phenomenon.name: Near-Death Experiences

aliases.name: Recalled Experience of Death (RED)
aliases.meaning: 2022 terminology proposed by NDE researchers for rigorous distinction

phenomenon.subcategory: Altered state of consciousness around clinical death

description.summary: Profound personal experiences associated with death or impending death, often reported by survivors of cardiac arrest and other life-threatening events. Common features include out-of-body sensations, passage through a tunnel, encounters with light and deceased relatives, and life review.
description.full: A Near-Death Experience (NDE) is a profound personal experience associated with death or impending death, typically occurring during reversible clinical death (most often cardiac arrest), severe trauma, or other life-threatening medical crises. Common features include detachment from the body, out-of-body experience (OBE), a sense of passage through a tunnel or darkness, encounter with a brilliant light, panoramic life review, meetings with deceased relatives or 'beings of light', feelings of peace and warmth, and sensations of levitation. The phenomenon was systematically described and named in 1975 by physician and philosopher Raymond Moody in his bestseller Life After Life, which identified fifteen recurring elements; earlier scholarly work includes Albert Heim's 1892 clinical observations of mountaineers' near-death experiences and Celia Green's 1968 analysis of out-of-body experience accounts. Major modern researchers include Bruce Greyson (whose 1983 Greyson NDE Scale is widely used), Kenneth Ring (1980 five-stage model), Pim van Lommel (whose 2001 prospective study of 344 cardiac-arrest survivors in The Lancet is among the most-cited works in the field), and Sam Parnia (lead investigator of the AWARE study, 2008–2012, of 2,060 cardiac-arrest events across 15 medical centres in the UK, Austria, and the United States). Estimates of prevalence range from roughly 10–20% of patients approaching death and 17% of critically ill patients. Proposed scientific explanations include cerebral hypoxia/anoxia, REM intrusion, temporal-parietal junction dysfunction, ketamine- and DMT-related neurochemistry, and dissociative responses to extreme stress; cultural framing (e.g. Christian angels, Hindu messengers of Yama) varies more than the underlying core features.

etymology.origin: The term 'near-death experience' was popularized by Raymond Moody in his 1975 book Life After Life.
etymology.meaning: Literally an experience occurring at or near the point of death.
etymology.first_use: 1975 (in Moody's Life After Life). Earlier clinical descriptions appear in Albert Heim's 1892 work.

related_phenomena.name: Out-of-Body Experience (OBE)
related_phenomena.description: A common element of NDEs, but also occurring outside near-death contexts

related_phenomena.name: Deathbed visions
related_phenomena.description: Visions reported by dying patients in their final hours

related_phenomena.name: Shared Death Experience
related_phenomena.description: NDE-like experiences reported by people present at another person's death

features.description: Subjective sense of being separate from one's physical body
Perception of viewing oneself and surroundings from a vantage point outside the body, sometimes including reportedly verifiable observations
Sensation of moving through a tunnel or dark space toward a light
Perception of an intense, often loving, light
Panoramic, often non-linear review of one's life events

features.feature: Encounter with deceased relatives or 'beings of light'
features.description: Meeting deceased family members or perceived spiritual beings

features.feature: Feelings of peace, warmth, and serenity
features.description: Profound emotional states reported as central to the experience

physical.morphology: Subjective phenomenology rather than physical morphology. Modern guidelines (2022) identify 51 common elements distinguishing authentic NDEs from related phenomena.

patterns: Most often reported following cardiac arrest, severe trauma, or other reversible clinical-death events
Cross-culturally consistent core features with culturally specific framing
Frequently produce lasting personality and worldview changes in experiencers

range.description: NDEs are reported worldwide and cross-culturally, with documented research in North America, Europe, and Asia.

first_recorded.source: Albert Heim's clinical study of mountaineers' near-death experiences (1892)

peak_activity_periods.description: Modern era of NDE research initiated by Raymond Moody's 1975 Life After Life
Major prospective hospital studies (van Lommel 2001; AWARE 2008–2012)

origins.cultural_roots: NDE-like accounts appear in religious and literary texts across many cultures (e.g. Plato's Republic Book X 'Myth of Er', medieval Christian visions, Tibetan Buddhist bardo literature).
origins.earliest_accounts: First clinical study by the Swiss geologist and physician Albert Heim in 1892, drawing on accounts from mountaineers who had survived falls.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely tied to religious ideas about the soul's passage at death; cross-cultural variation in framing the core experience.

timeline.event: Albert Heim publishes the first clinical study of near-death experiences, drawn from accounts of survivors of falls in the Alps
timeline.significance: Earliest formal clinical study of the phenomenon

timeline.event: Celia Green analyzes 400 out-of-body experience accounts
timeline.significance: Foundational empirical study of OBEs, a core NDE feature

timeline.event: Raymond Moody publishes Life After Life, identifying fifteen recurring NDE elements and coining the modern term
timeline.significance: Founding text of the modern field

timeline.event: Kenneth Ring publishes Life at Death, proposing a five-stage continuum model for NDEs
Bruce Greyson publishes the Greyson NDE Scale
timeline.significance: Standardised diagnostic instrument that remains in wide use

timeline.event: Pim van Lommel and colleagues publish a prospective study of 344 cardiac-arrest survivors across 10 Dutch hospitals in The Lancet
timeline.significance: Among the most-cited prospective studies of NDEs
timeline.source: van Lommel, P. et al. (2001), The Lancet

timeline.event: Sam Parnia and colleagues publish results of the AWARE study (2008–2012) of 2,060 cardiac-arrest events at 15 medical centres
timeline.significance: Largest prospective multi-centre study of NDEs to date

timeline.event: Multidisciplinary panel proposes 'Recalled Experience of Death' (RED) terminology and identifies 51 common elements
timeline.significance: Effort to standardise rigorous diagnostic criteria

history.modern_era: Contemporary NDE research centres on prospective hospital-based studies of cardiac-arrest survivors (especially van Lommel's 2001 cohort and the AWARE / AWARE II studies under Sam Parnia), neurobiological correlates of NDE-like states, and rigorous distinction between authentic NDEs, dissociative experiences, and confabulation.

notable.name: van Lommel et al. (2001), The Lancet — prospective NDE study

location.description: Ten Dutch hospitals (consortium led by Pim van Lommel)

notable.description: A prospective study of 344 cardiac-arrest survivors at ten Dutch hospitals comparing patients who reported NDEs against those who did not. The study reported that one patient accurately recalled details of resuscitation events from an out-of-body perspective, and follow-ups documented lasting personality and worldview changes among NDE experiencers.

credibility.notes: One of the most influential prospective NDE studies; some methodological details have been debated, but the publication itself is well-documented.

sources: van Lommel, P. et al. (2001), The Lancet 358:2039–2045

notable.name: AWARE study (Parnia et al., 2014) — multi-centre prospective study

location.description: 15 medical centres in the UK, Austria, and the United States

notable.description: From 2008 to 2012, the AWARE study reviewed 2,060 cardiac-arrest events. Of 140 survivors, 101 completed questionnaires, of whom approximately 9% reported experiences classifiable as NDEs; two patients were reported to have demonstrated verifiable visual or auditory awareness during cardiac arrest. The study attempted to test out-of-body claims using hidden visual targets in resuscitation areas, with negative results for the targets themselves.

factors: Largest prospective multi-centre NDE study to date
credibility.notes: Confirmed that NDEs are reported by a measurable minority of survivors but did not validate the hidden-target test of OBE.

sources: Parnia, S. et al. (2014), AWARE study results, Resuscitation

documentary.name: Greyson NDE Scale
documentary.description: 16-item validated questionnaire for assessing the depth and content of NDEs, developed by psychiatrist Bruce Greyson in 1983.
documentary.analysis: Widely adopted across NDE research; modern critics note the instrument can produce false positives by labeling non-NDE mystical experiences as NDEs.

paranormal.name: Survival of consciousness
paranormal.description: Hypothesis that NDEs evidence the survival of consciousness independent of brain activity, and represent a glimpse of an afterlife or non-material reality.
evidence_cited: Reported veridical perceptions during cardiac arrest
Apparent NDEs during periods of greatly reduced or absent measurable brain activity

scientific.name: Cerebral hypoxia and anoxia
scientific.description: NDE features are produced by acute reduction of cerebral oxygen during cardiac arrest or other crises, generating tunnel vision, light perception, and altered consciousness.
evidence_cited: Comparable phenomena under high-G force loss of consciousness (G-LOC)
Visual and cognitive symptoms of hypoxia

scientific.name: Neurochemical models (endorphins, ketamine, DMT)
scientific.description: NDE phenomenology is plausibly mediated by endogenous opioids, ketamine-like NMDA antagonism, and/or DMT-like serotonergic effects released under extreme stress.
evidence_cited: Phenomenological similarity between NDEs and ketamine, DMT, and Salvia divinorum experiences

scientific.name: Temporal-parietal junction dysfunction
scientific.description: Disruption of the temporal-parietal junction can produce out-of-body sensations, suggesting a neurological substrate for NDE OBEs.
evidence_cited: Direct cortical stimulation experiments producing OBE-like sensations

scientific.name: REM intrusion
scientific.description: NDE features may arise from intrusion of REM-state phenomena into waking consciousness near death.
evidence_cited: Higher reported rates of REM-related sleep phenomena among NDE experiencers

skeptical.name: Confabulation and expectancy effects
skeptical.description: Many reported NDEs may be partially or wholly confabulated under stress, shaped by cultural expectation and reinforced by retelling.
evidence_cited: Failures of the AWARE hidden-target test

skeptical.name: Critique of Greyson Scale specificity
skeptical.description: Modern scholars argue the Greyson NDE Scale's vague terminology (e.g. 'unearthly place', 'mystical feelings') admits false positives, conflating authentic NDEs with other anomalous experiences.
evidence_cited: 2022 NDE-research consensus document proposing the RED terminology

folklore.beliefs: NDEs are interpreted across many traditions as evidence of an afterlife, journeys to gods or psychopomps, or ego-dissolution states.

literature: Consciousness Beyond Life — Pim van Lommel (2010)

researchers.name: Raymond Moody
researchers.contribution: Identified 15 foundational NDE elements; coined the modern term

researchers.name: Bruce Greyson
researchers.contribution: Greyson NDE Scale (1983) and decades of clinical research

researchers.name: Pim van Lommel
researchers.contribution: Prospective study of 344 cardiac-arrest survivors in The Lancet (2001)

researchers.name: Sam Parnia
researchers.contribution: Lead investigator of the AWARE and AWARE II studies

organizations.name: International Association for Near-Death Studies (IANDS)
organizations.focus: Research, support, and education on NDEs

organizations.name: Division of Perceptual Studies, University of Virginia
organizations.focus: Academic research on NDEs and related phenomena

research.ongoing_studies: Active areas include the AWARE II prospective cardiac-arrest study, neurobiological investigations of NDE correlates, and ongoing methodological refinement (RED criteria, 2022).
